content: Testing algorithms that incorporate Western blotting or line immunoassays have been associated with several challenges. These include: 1. A higher frequency of indeterminate results, necessitating additional follow-up testing for clients after a 14-day period. 2. Prolonged turnaround times between the initial test and the delivery of a definitive HIV diagnosis. 3. Increased rates of loss to follow-up and delays in linking individuals to appropriate treatment. 4. Higher costs and reduced acceptability among both clients and healthcare providers. Programs transitioning away from Western blotting or line immunoassays can adopt alternative HIV rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). The selection of new assays should be based on their performance in combination with other assays within the testing algorithm. Moving away from these older methods allows for the provision of HIV testing services (HTS) to a larger population with fewer resources. Efforts must be made to support and redefine the role of laboratories, enabling them to take on broader responsibilities in areas such as supervisory support and quality assurance. Transitioning from Western blotting or line immunoassays requires changes in national policies and the training of healthcare staff. These changes should align with broader initiatives to scale up rapid antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and improve access to HIV prevention services. Engaging communities and stakeholders in this process is critical to ensure success. Abandoning Western blotting is expected to enhance equity and increase the uptake of HTS. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that HIV testing algorithms be verified before widespread implementation. Properly chosen combinations of RDTs or integrated immunoassays and RDTs can deliver reliable results at a lower cost. Verification of testing algorithms serves several purposes: It empowers national programs to select products tailored to their specific contexts, such as the type of testing providers, environmental conditions, and facility workloads. It generates data on the optimal combination of assays for use in the WHO testing strategy, accounting for potential cross-reactivity among assays. It allows national programs to familiarize themselves with selected products before large-scale procurement. Verification should be conducted every three to five years to incorporate innovations and the latest diagnostic tests, ensuring alignment with program priorities. Post-market surveillance is a vital component of maintaining the quality of testing services. Testing algorithms must be continuously monitored for effectiveness, particularly for cases of HIV misdiagnosis. Data collection should focus on the rates of inconclusive HIV status reports and invalid test results, with an acceptable threshold of no more than 5%. Complaints related to diagnostic products should be reported to both the assay manufacturer and the national regulatory authority as part of post-market surveillance. Quality assurance is essential for accurate HIV diagnosis in all programs. Implementing quality management systems (QMS) is a requirement for all forms of HTS, whether conducted in laboratories, healthcare facilities, community settings, or through self-testing. In vitro diagnostic medical devices (IVDs) must meet national regulatory standards, and WHO conducts independent prequalification assessments of IVDs, particularly HIV RDTs, for use in various settings. External quality assurance (EQA) programs, including proficiency testing (PT) for HIV diagnostic tests, are a priority to ensure the accuracy and reliability of test results. HTS providers may need to refer individuals to other sites for additional testing. Consistent, clear, confidential, accurate, and timely record-keeping is critical at both the initial testing site and the referral site. Accurate HIV diagnosis is a cornerstone of any HIV program, particularly in the context of treat all recommendations for immediate ART initiation. Care must be taken to avoid misdiagnosing individuals without HIV as HIV-positive, which could lead to unnecessary lifelong ART. Misdiagnosis of HIV status, whether false-positive or false-negative, has been reported. Studies have highlighted suboptimal performance of testing strategies and algorithms that deviate from WHO recommendations, as well as errors by providers.
